newsitem.title: LUXEMBOURG: Court says travel agents subject to VAT in multiple states.
newsitem.headline: Court says travel agents subject to VAT in multiple states.

text.p: The European Court of Justice said on Thursday travel agencies operating in more than one member state may be subject to multiple VAT jurisdiction if the secondary office meets the definition of a fixed establishment.

On the face of it, the court's decision contradicts the Sixth VAT directive's special scheme for travel agencies. That scheme permits VAT collecton where an agency is established, in recognition of the special circumstances of doing business in multiple locations.

The Danish parent travel agency, DFDS A/S, argued the British excise office could not tax its subsidiary, DFDS Ltd., on package tours sold for the parent, under the establishment rule. After the VAT Tribunal agreed, the tax office appealed to the High Court.

The issue is complicated by a variety of member state tax rules for travel agents - Denmark has exempted travel services from VAT, Britain has not. The court noted that "systematic reliance on the place where the supplier has established his business could lead to distortion in business."
The court followed reasoning submitted by Italy and the Commission to establish a test for determining when sufficient independence exists to merit VAT collection where services are supplied.

A separate legal personality would not be sufficient to establish independence from the parent, the court said. In fact evidence of a wholly owned subsidiary acting in an auxiliary capacity would strengthen the Danish parent's arguments.
But if the subsidiary operates with some level of independence, and has the "human and technical characteristic of a fixed establishment", it is subject to VAT on services where it is located.
The threshold to determine how many employees, computers or telephones suffice to meet a definition of fixed establishment was not set out by the court, as those facts were not discussed.
However, the court possessed those facts and recommended to the High Court that the British subsidiary be taxed as a fixed establishment, under British VAT rules.

The agency agreement between the two companies, DFDS A/S and DFDS Ltd, designates the subsidiary as a "general sales and port agent and as a "central booking office for the UK and Ireland for all the passenger services" of the parent.

THE COURT hereby rules

Article 26(2) of the Sixth Council directive (77/388/EEC) of 17 May 1977 on the harmonization of the laws of the member states relating to turnover taxes - Common system of value added tax: uniform basis of assessment, is to be interpreted as meaning that, where a tour operator established in one member state provides services to travellers through the intermediary of a company operating as an agent in another member state, VAT is payable on those services in the latter state if that compnay, which acts as a mere auxiliary organ of the tour operator, has the human and technical resources characteristic of a fixed establishment.
